title: Chapter 9.  Article 370 — Origins, Provisions & the Old Special Constitutional Status

blocks.content: Article 370 is the single most important constitutional topic in the entire J&K syllabus, since its 2019 abrogation (covered in Chapter 13) represents the dividing line between the region's 'old status' and 'new status' — the specific comparison the exam most wants candidates to master. This chapter covers what Article 370 actually said and why it existed; Chapter 13 covers its removal.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Article 370 granted a temporary special constitutional status to Jammu & Kashmir in Part XXI of the Indian Constitution.
Parliamentary law-making powers were initially limited to Defense, Foreign Affairs, Finance, and Communications.
Extension of other Union laws required the concurrence or ratification of the J&K State Government/Constituent Assembly.
Article 35A was empowered via Presidential Order under Article 370 to define permanent residents and grant exclusive rights.
Between the 1950s and 2019, successive Presidential Orders systematically extended various central provisions and jurisdiction to the state.

blocks.content: Article 370, titled 'Temporary provisions with respect to the State of Jammu and Kashmir', was incorporated into the Constitution of India as it was being drafted in 1949, reflecting the special circumstances of J&K's accession: unlike most princely states (which acceded fully and were then integrated administratively through separate Instruments of Merger), J&K's Maharaja had acceded only on the three subjects of Defence, External Affairs and Communications, with the expectation — reflected in Mountbatten's accompanying statement — that the final constitutional relationship would be settled later, potentially in consultation with the people via a plebiscite.

The Article was drafted primarily under the guidance of Sheikh Abdullah (then head of J&K's interim administration, negotiating on behalf of the state) and N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar (a member of the Indian Constituent Assembly and former Diwan of the state), reflecting a negotiated compromise between the Indian Union and J&K's political leadership rather than a unilateral central imposition.
Article 370 — Origins, Provisions & the Old Special Constitutional Status

The word 'Temporary' in the Article's title has been the subject of extensive legal and political debate over the decades — some viewed it as intended to be a transitional arrangement pending eventual full integration or a plebiscite, while others (including many in Kashmir) viewed it as a permanent guarantee of special autonomous status; this interpretive dispute became central to the political and legal arguments both for and against the Article's eventual abrogation in 2019.

★ EXAM POINT: Article 370 fell under Part XXI of the Constitution, titled 'Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions' — the same Part that contains various other special provisions for different states, though Article 370's scope for J&K was by far the most extensive of any of them.

rows: Fully integrated UT status / Same as rest of India
Separate Constitution and separate State Flag
Uniform Indian citizenship rights across all citizens

cells: Limited automatic applicability of the Indian Constitution

Only Article 1 (defining India as a Union of States) and Article 370 itself applied automatically to J&K; all other constitutional provisions applied only via specific Presidential Orders, generally requiring the concurrence of the state government (and, for matters beyond the original Instrument of Accession's three subjects, potentially requiring ratification by the state's own Constituent Assembly)
J&K adopted its own separate state Constitution in 1957 (drafted by a specially convened J&K Constituent Assembly), governing matters not covered by the Indian Constitution's limited applicability

Parliament could legislate for J&K only on subjects in the Union and Concurrent Lists corresponding to the original three acceded subjects (Defence, External Affairs, Communications) without the state government's concurrence; other subjects required concurrence

J&K historically had its own state flag (alongside the national flag) and, until later constitutional amendments and Presidential Orders altered the terminology, used the distinct title 'Sadar-i-Riyasat' (Head of State) and 'Prime Minister' for its own top constitutional office-holders (later changed to 'Governor' and 'Chief Minister', aligning more closely with other Indian states)
Article 370 provided the constitutional gateway through which Article 35A (permanent-resident/property-rights provisions, see Chapter 10) was inserted by a 1954 Presidential Order

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: J&K having its OWN separate state Constitution (1957) alongside the Indian Constitution was one of the most distinctive and frequently tested features of the pre-2019 'old status' — no other Indian state had this arrangement, making it a strong marker of J&K's exceptional constitutional position within the Union.
Gradual Erosion & Extension of Central Provisions (1950s-2019)

Although Article 370 in principle preserved wide autonomy for J&K, a long series of Presidential Orders issued over the decades (each nominally requiring state-government concurrence) progressively extended the application of central laws and constitutional provisions to the state, a process critics on different sides characterised either as 'gradual erosion of special status' or as 'gradual, legitimate integration', depending on political viewpoint.

The 1952 Delhi Agreement between the Government of India and Sheikh Abdullah's state government formalised several key terms of the relationship (including the adoption of the Indian national flag alongside the state flag, and the extension of Indian citizenship and fundamental rights with specified modifications), representing an early, consensual phase of this integration process before the political relationship later became more strained.

items: Article 370 was classified under 'Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions' in Part XXI of the Constitution.
Presidential Orders (e.g., the 1954 Order) were the primary mechanism used to extend constitutional provisions to J&K.
Central laws outside Defense, External Affairs, Communications, and Finance required state concurrence before being applicable.

blocks.content: By the time of its 2019 abrogation, several hundred Presidential Orders and numerous Central Acts had already been extended to J&K over the preceding seven decades, meaning that in practical/legal terms, the extent of J&K's 'special status' had already narrowed considerably even before the Article's formal removal — an important nuance that avoids over-simplifying the 2019 change as a single dramatic reversal from full autonomy to none.

items: Article 370 ('Temporary provisions...') incorporated into the Constitution in 1949, reflecting J&K's limited-subject accession (Defence, External Affairs, Communications only).
Drafted primarily via negotiation between Sheikh Abdullah and N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar.
J&K had its OWN separate state Constitution (adopted 1957) — a uniquely distinctive feature among Indian states.
1952 Delhi Agreement formalised early terms: Indian flag alongside state flag, Indian citizenship, modified fundamental rights application.
By 2019, extensive Presidential Orders/Central Acts had ALREADY been extended to J&K over 7 decades — the 2019 abrogation (Chapter 13) completed rather than solely initiated this integration process.
